The basics

What is Melvor Idle 2?

It's the direct sequel to Melvor Idle (2021), rebuilt from scratch in the Godot engine by Australian studio Games by Malcs — this time self-published, with no Jagex involvement. The original distilled RuneScape's skilling and combat into a menu-driven idle game; the sequel keeps that idea and expands almost every part of it.

The one-sentence pitch

You train skills with a click or a tap. Every skill feeds the others: logs become fires and arrows, ore becomes bars, bars become armour, fish become food, and food keeps you alive in combat. Progress continues offline at the same speed as online, so a busy schedule is not a disadvantage — it's the intended way to play.

New in the sequel: story-driven Quests with quest bosses, a reworked combat system, Mastery Guilds (a task-based replacement for the old per-item Mastery), an in-game Codex that explains every item and mechanic, a day/night cycle with weather, and five skills that didn't exist in the first game.

New to idle games?

"Idle" doesn't mean "nothing to do." It means your decisions are about what to do next and what to queue up before you log off — not fast clicking. The fun is in planning loops: "If I fish tonight, I can cook tomorrow, smith with the ore from the weekend, then finally take on that dungeon."

How to play

The core loop, in five steps

Almost everything in Melvor Idle 2 is this loop repeating at bigger scales. Learn it once and the whole game makes sense.

1

Pick a skill

Choose any skill from the menu — say, Fishing — then pick an action inside it, like catching Raw Shrimp at level 1. Hit start. That's it: you're training.

2

Watch the bank fill

Every action takes a few seconds and drops items into your Bank (your inventory). XP goes into the skill with each action. Items stack, so long sessions build serious stockpiles.

3

Spend it in another skill

Turn raw materials into something better: cook the fish, smelt the ore, fletch the logs. Processed items are worth more XP, more gold, or are usable in combat.

4

Gear up & fight

Equip the weapons, armour and food you made, pick a combat area, and fight automatically. Loot, gold and Slayer tasks push you toward tougher areas, dungeons and bosses.

5

Log off — keep progressing

Close the game and your last action keeps running offline at full speed. When you return, an offline summary (and the new Event Log) shows exactly what you earned.

Levels, XP and the 120 cap

Each skill levels independently from 1 to 120 (up from 99 in the original base game). Higher levels unlock better actions — better trees, ores, fish, monsters and recipes — which give faster XP. There's no character level gating you: if a skill is unlocked, you can train it.

In the October demo every skill stopped at 60; in Early Access (from 17 Nov 2026) the cap is 99. The 100–120 stretch arrives with the full v1.0 release plan.

Mastery Guilds (new system)

Melvor Idle 2 replaces the first game's per-item Mastery with Mastery Guilds — one for skilling and one for combat. Instead of grinding one item thousands of times, you complete guild tasks tied to each skill to earn its mastery rewards and bonuses. It's designed to reward variety over repetition.

Quests give you direction

Unlike the largely sandbox original, Melvor Idle 2 has a main storyline told through dialogue-driven quests. Act 1 is in the demo. Quests teach mechanics as you go, send you into unique skilling content, and pit you against quest bosses — following them is the easiest way to learn the game without a guide open.

The Codex is your in-game wiki

Stuck on where an item comes from? The built-in Codex lets you search any content, read how a mechanic works, and see an item's Uses & Sources. Pair it with Current Action Tracking — live XP/hr, items/hr and combat rates for whatever you're doing — to compare training methods without spreadsheets.

Beginner roadmap

Your first week: a starter route that works

There's no wrong way to play an idle game, but new players often stall by jumping into combat with no food or gear. This route — adapted from the original game's well-tested beginner advice to Melvor Idle 2 — builds your supply lines first, then fights. It worked in the demo (cap 60) and carries into Early Access (cap 99). For earning, pair it with the gold guide below: quests first for lump sums, then Thieving once Cooking hits 10.

  1. Hour 1

    Follow the quests, then fish

    Play through the opening story quests — they're the tutorial. Then open Fishing and catch Raw Shrimp (your level-1 option). Fish are the backbone of early food, and Fishing needs no tools or supplies to start.

  2. Day 1

    Cook everything, chop and mine on the side

    • Cooking: cook your raw fish into food. Never fight without a full food slot.
    • Woodcutting: start on Normal Trees, move to Oak when unlocked. Logs feed Firemaking, Fletching and Crafting.
    • Mining: mine Copper and Tin first — together they smelt into Bronze.
    • Firemaking: burn spare logs for easy early XP and to clear bank space.
  3. Day 2

    Smith your first kit

    Smelt Bronze Bars in Smithing and craft a bronze weapon and armour set. This is your ticket into real combat. Keep mining as you level — Iron and then Steel are the next gear tiers, and Smithing XP is some of the most useful in the game because your gear literally comes from it.

  4. Day 2–3

    Start Farming and Ranching early — they're passive

    Farming (rebuilt for the sequel) and the new Ranching skill produce resources over time once set up. Plant crops and set up animals — cows, pigs, sheep, chickens and worms in the alpha — as soon as you can, then mostly forget them. Every hour you delay starting a passive skill is production you never get back. Check the skill explorer below for what each one does.

  5. Day 3–4

    First combat: one style, weak enemies, full belly

    Pick Melee first (see the Combat section) — its gear is the easiest to make yourself. Fight the weakest monsters in the first combat area, eat when your health drops, and loot everything. Work through your first Slayer tasks and save gold instead of spending it: bank space and upgrades get expensive fast.

  6. Day 5–7

    Broaden to ~30 in everything, then specialise

    The classic Melvor advice still holds: get most skills to around level 30 to learn how they interlock, visit your Mastery Guilds and pick up their tasks, and only then choose a focus — a combat push, a money-making skill like Thieving or Fishing, or questing through the story. By now your offline sessions should be planned: always log off doing the longest, most useful action you have.

About this roadmap & honesty note

Melvor Idle 2 is still in alpha/demo, and full per-skill mechanics for the sequel haven't all been published yet. Steps above that come from the original game's beginner guides (food first, gear tiers, "30 in everything") are labelled series fundamentals — they carry over because the sequel keeps the same skill loop — while demo contents, skill names, caps and dates are confirmed sequel facts, sourced at the bottom of this page.

Gold making · Updated 17 Nov 2026 — Early Access launch day

How to make gold in Melvor Idle 2

There is no trading, auction house or flipping — Melvor Idle 2 is single-player, so every coin comes from merchant sales, quest rewards and monster GP drops. The ranked consensus below is from the dedicated MI2 guides at melvoridle-2.wiki and melvor2.com, cross-checked against the official Steam launch patch notes (17 Nov 2026).

Read this first: there is no verified Early Access GP/hour yet

No source publishes a verified EA GP/hour for any method. melvoridle-2.wiki says explicitly that “a number copied from the demo is a number waiting to be wrong” and ranks by stage instead; melvor2.com's Thieving table leaves its GP Rate column blank (“—”) for every bracket. All unit sell prices on this page are from the October 2026 demo game files (build 26316041 / 0.11.2, via melvor2.com) — pre–Early Access balance. The launch patch buffed several early gold sources (see launch changes below), so treat demo prices as a floor and order-of-magnitude guide, not EA rates. Do not use Melvor Idle 1 rates (e.g. Thieving Princess ~24.7m/hr or Dragon Javelins ~9.5m/hr on the MI1 wiki) — different game, different economy.

The skills, ranked for gold

  1. Thieving — best reliable cash at every stage

    The only skill that pays GP directly per action, plus seeds and unique drops (jewellery, gear, bars). Low setup, no material consumption — your only cost is food. Weakness: fail / stun / jail risk. It is the first dedicated money skill and remains the late-game default. melvoridle-2.wiki FAQ; navgame.org.

  2. Fishing + Cooking — best starter & by-product income

    Fish is food and gold. Cooked fish sells for roughly 1.5–1.9× raw (Shrimp 5→8, Sardine 13→22, Herring 15→28, Perch 26→48, Pike 65→99, Lobster 80→113 GP). Fishing specials (e.g. Rope at Quiet Bend) add value. Needs nothing beyond Woodcutting 2 to unlock — and it stocks the food that Thieving and combat burn.

  3. Mining + Smithing — best processing loop

    Ore → bar → weapon roughly doubles to triples value at each step (Iron Ore 6 → Iron Bar 12 → Iron Sword 48 GP; Mithril Ore 18 → Bar 56 → Sword 161 GP). Costs coal and Smithing time. Keep ore for your own gear and quests first.

  4. Combat / Slayer — good, but costed

    Kill GP scales with monster level (Golbin 10–40 → Rainbow Slime L28 28–110 GP/kill) plus sellable drops and dungeon chests (Hobgolbin Chest 400 GP). Early Slayer GP (Slimes, Bees) was buffed at launch. Net profit = drops − food/potions, and it is not AFK-safe without Auto Eat / a food stock.

  5. Woodcutting — steady low-tier seller

    Mahogany Log 46 GP (L55), Maple 33 (L45), Teak 25, Willow 17, Oak 6 GP. Mainly feeds Firemaking and Fletching — sell surplus only.

  6. Crafting / Runecrafting / Herblore — value-adders, not primary earners

    Crafting jewellery (Topaz → Emerald) had its sale price increased at EA launch; early Wands and Staves (Runecrafting) likewise — no amounts were published. Herblore: potions beat herbs, so do not sell herbs if you are training Herblore. These skills pay best when their outputs feed your own progression.

  7. Astrology & Agility — multipliers and utility, not income

    Astrology gives permanent bonuses to nearly every skill and no direct gold — train it to raise every other method's rate. Agility gives utility/buffs in MI2 EA with no published MI2 GP figure; do not import MI1's ~5m/hr Agility figure.

  8. Farming / Ranching / Hunting / Beastcrafting — parallel background income

    None is a primary active method in any guide found — they run alongside other training, which is exactly why you start them early. Farming was reworked (orchard trees, flowers with passive bonuses, pests/disease/watering, compost bins, Grain Mill, built-in auto plant/harvest/compost). Ranching animals produce hourly while you train something else (Sheep L1, Chicken L5, Cow L15, Pig, Elk L55). Hunting (needs Crafting 3) → Beastcrafting (Hunting 15 + 1 Bushland Rabbit) turns animal materials into gear. Summoning is planned before v1.0 and Cartography is not on the 29-skill v1.0 list — neither contributes to EA gold.

Spend your first cash in this order

1. Bank slots — +20 slots = 5,000 GP at skill level 20; +50 combat storage = 25,000 GP after 10 Hobgolbin Camp clears. Bank slots are permanent.
2. Seeds — buy seeds with first cash, after bank slots.
3. Weapon upgrade — a weapon accelerates every subsequent hour. Copper Axe/Pickaxe cost 2,000 GP + 25 Copper Bars at level 5.

Order and prices: melvoridle-2.wiki / melvor2.com guides, demo values.

Launch patch — 17 Nov 2026 (Steam News)

Balance changes were deliberately light, targeting “increasing early game GP sources”:

• Quest GP rewards doubled — players who already completed quests are granted the difference on load.
• Sale price increased for craftable Jewellery from Topaz to Emerald, and for early Wands and Staves in Runecrafting (no amounts published).
• GP rewards increased from early Slayer monsters (Slimes, Bees, etc. — no amounts published).
• Feathers nerfed: 4 GP → 1 GP.
• Compost / Super Compost buffed (now a higher bonus than Fertiliser) — an indirect Farming buff.
• Also: 4 new Mastery Guild ranks, Act 2 quests, Astrology/Herblore/Agility unlocked, Ranching enclosure direct upgrades, a “Reach Level” stop condition.

No post-launch hotfix existed as of 17 Nov 2026, 19:23 UTC. The Early Access roadmap is due the following week — re-check Steam News after the first week.

Sell vs. keep

Sell: surplus fish (especially cooked), surplus logs/ore/bars/weapons above your gear needs, cut gems only if Crafting is not in your plan, thieved jewellery and duplicate gear (Silver Topaz Ring 97 GP, Copper Platebody 127 GP), dungeon chests (Hobgolbin Chest 400 GP). Always process before selling — bars > ore, cooked > raw, potions > herbs, weapons > bars.

Keep: food for combat/thieving (500k GP and no food means rebuying at a worse rate), materials for the next recipe or quest — check the Codex before selling anything, and never sell quest items — plus herbs for Herblore, ore for Smithing, and seeds.

Traps & nerfed methods

• Feather farming is dead: feathers dropped 4 GP → 1 GP at launch, so “Rip Giant Chicken” is no longer a money method.
• Don't chase a demo-era GP/h — the launch build changed levels, items and monster tables.
• Don't buy food if you can fish it; don't sell inputs to a skill you're actively training.
• Don't hoard thousands of low-tier materials — 5 of each common material covers most quests.
• MI1 traps that do not transfer: Gem Gloves mining, Dragon Javelin fletching, and the Leprechaun+Monkey Thieving synergy are not confirmed in MI2 EA — don't save up for them on MI1 advice. There is also no Township in MI2 — MI1's big passive-income town builder is absent from both the 25-skill EA roster and the 29-skill v1.0 plan.

Offline progression & gold

Up to 24 hours is replayed tick-by-tick when you return; time beyond 24h is lost. The Welcome Back screen lists per-skill cards with levels, XP, items gained and hourly rate. Actions stop when materials run out — a 10-hour absence with 20 minutes of materials earns 20 minutes of progress; the game does not create ingredients, so set a stop condition if you don't want a craft to run dry, and always leave an action with enough inputs for the time away. The offline rate matches online for the chosen action — you just can't switch actions while away. Ranching is the exception: its hourly production runs alongside whatever else you're doing and gets its own Welcome Back card, making it the best “set and forget” parallel stream overnight. Open question: whether Thieving/Combat run offline in MI2, and whether any offline penalty applies beyond the 24h limit, is not documented in the MI2 sources found — in MI1 they needed an explicit offline toggle, so check the in-game setting rather than assuming.

Sequel changes

Melvor Idle 2 vs. the original

This is a full rebuild, not a remaster — new engine, new systems, and a level cap that goes well past the original's. If you're coming from Melvor Idle 1, here's what actually changed:

Original's Beginner's Guide ↗

System requirements are tiny

Steam lists minimums of 1 GB RAM and integrated graphics on Windows (2 GB RAM on macOS/Linux) with 2–4 GB storage. If your machine can run a browser comfortably, it can run Melvor Idle 2 — fitting for a game designed to tick along in the background of a busy life.

Hard-won lessons

Six beginner mistakes to skip

1. Fighting without food

Combat with an empty food slot ends one way. Cook first, fight second — every time, no exceptions for "just one quick kill."

2. Starting passive skills late

Farming and Ranching produce while you do everything else — including sleeping. Set them up on day one, not week three.

3. Selling everything you gather

Logs, ore and fish look like gold, but they're worth more as XP and gear in other skills. Sell surplus and finished products, not your supply chain.

4. Ignoring your bank

Bank space is finite and upgrades cost gold. Use MI2's tagging, tab names and placeholders from the start instead of drowning in unstacked clutter later.

5. Training one skill to 99 first

Skills multiply each other. A rounded character around level 30 everywhere progresses faster — and dies less — than a one-skill specialist.

6. Logging off idle

Offline progression only pays if you left an action running. Before closing the game, always ask: "What's my character doing for the next 8 hours?"
